newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Dlr tumbles to 7-month low, Eurobourses mixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dlr tumbles to 7-month low, Eurobourses mixed.

text.p: The dollar recovered slightly after tumbling to a seven-month low against the yen on Wednesday amid renewed fears of U.S.-Japan trade tensions, while European bourses were mixed after a unsteady start on Wall Street.

Paris stocks climbed by more than one per percent as worries receded about disruption of the timetable for the launch of Europe's single currency. Frankfurt also made healthy gains, but London, after briefly opening at a record level, dipped into the minus column.

Most of the action was in currency markets. The dollar regained some poise after plunging to its lowest level since November 1996, hit by concerns that a burgeoning Japanese current account surplus would cause trade friction between Washington and Tokyo.
The dollar slumped to 110.70 yen in early trade before clawing its way up to 111. 27 yen later, still well below 112.61 seen in late Europe on Tuesday.
Currency traders were worried that Washington would take issue with Tokyo's widening trade surplus before next week's meeting of the world's largest industrial nations.
U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers triggered the slump in the dollar after he said that Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
His comments hit home, coming after a report which showed Japan's current account and trade surplus surged in April.
"The U.S. seems to be stepping up the war of words and it looks like we are going to test the 110 (yen) levels," said Steve Hannah, the director of research at IBJ International .

Senior Japanese officials tried to mount a damage limitation exercise. Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that Japan would act to combat excessive currency swings, while Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita called for more stability.
But their remarks cut little ice with traders because they have failed so far to stop the dollar tumbling over 13 percent from a four-and-a-half-year high of 127.46 yen in little more than a month.

The dollar's 60 percent rebound from the post-World War Two low of 79.76 set in April 1995 has boosted Japanese exporters' competitiveness against their U.S. rivals and fuelled the increase in Japan's trade surpluses.

While Mitsuzuka said Japan's trade and services surplus was unlikely to rise significantly in the medium term, he also said the surpluses were likely to be discussed when Group of Seven leading industrial nations meet in Denver on June 20-22.
In equity markets, trading was mixed, with London, which closed at a new peak on Tuesday, especially volatile.
Its benchmark FTSE 100 index shot into record ground at the start, touching 4759.3 points on news of a possible bid for Energy Group Plc, dealers said.

But investors soon lost their nerve. Stocks shed all their gains and were down 0.4 percent by mid-afternoon. No help came from the unsteady start in Wall Street , which closed at its third consecutive peak on Tuesday.

Paris was the best performer of the day, with bonds and stocks moving ahead as European Union policy-makers voiced optimism that differences over a budget stability pact for countries inside monetary union could be resolved in time for an EU summit in Amsterdam next week.
"The market really wants to believe France will sign (the stability pact in Amsterdam)," Credit Agricole Indosuez economist Arnaud Mares said. "I think they need to be more cautious."

Stocks and bonds lost ground after the new Socialist government asked on Monday for a delay in signing the pact and said it could not accept the deal agreed by the previous conservative administration unless more stress was put on fighting unemployment.

The markets got a lift after Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said on Tuesday the French government had told him it did not have to wait to present its policies to parliament on June 19 before ratifying the pact.

In Frankfurt, floor trade ended with modest gains but traders said jitters about European monetary union were still a factor and prices were just a trace softer on the computerised IBIS index by mid-afternoon.
CURRENCIES AT 1430 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7160 marks and 111.27 yen compared with 1.7186 marks and 112.61 yen on Tuesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1430 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 14.5 points at 4,725.6.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 18.67 points at 2,682.85.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index ended up 12.42 at 3,677.43.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed in the afternoon at $343.80 compared with Tuesday's close of $343.75. Silver was unchanged at $4.79.
